<reason>Both sides ran coherent, well-shaped cases: B on completion risk, forgone earnings, and portable licenses; A on scale, selection, and the slope of general human capital. A won because it fixed the decision rule to the word "expanding" and then landed two hits B never squarely neutralized. First, the instrument point: the motion compares subsidies, so B's recurring "debt compounding" villain largely misfires, and B kept repeating it even after A flagged it ("you keep prosecuting loans in a debate about aid"). Second, the scale/agency point: B's own answer that public money "bribes away the bottleneck" and that recession-proof slots come from hospitals, utilities and public construction let A characterize the plan's reach as decided one HR screen at a time and anchored in employers government already controls. B's rebuttals were good — the "selection after tuition is crueler than selection before pay" reframe was its sharpest moment, and it forced A to concede a lot about marginal-student completion — but B answered gain-per-person well and reach-per-cohort only partially. A also handled B's pressure questions directly (fraction of a large number times a large premium; underemployment as a first-job condition), whereas B's answer on compulsion effectively conceded voluntariness. A's cost: its second rebuttal ran over and was clipped mid-weighing, which trims the margin, though the closing recovered the framing cleanly.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's turn-4 pincer: if apprentices produce value from month one, firms should already run them at scale unsubsidized, so money is not the binding constraint — combined with the point that "employer-linked" means employer-selected, so the very students B says college fails are the ones contractors pass over. B's reply (hassle costs, intermediaries, reliability screening) was competent but conceded that reach depends on voluntary firm appetite, which A then converted into its closing weighing.</best_rebuttal>
